items.descriptionOriginal: Jane Austen published four novels during her lifetime, with two more appearing after her death. Then there are the numerous poems , plays, and parodies she wrote in her youth, along with the lengthy letters she continued writing throughout her life. Even more impressive than the output, however, is the lasting influence of Austen’s work. For many writers, that kind of creative consistency comes with a routine. Writers throughout history have developed their own rituals for getting into the right headspace to work, whether that means writing at the same time every day, working in a particular place, or starting the day with an activity that has nothing to do with writing. Austen had her own version of a creative warm-up: before settling in to write, she would sit down at the pianoforte. Jane Austen started her creative day with music During her years at Chawton Cottage, which happened to be one of the most productive periods of her career, Austen played the pianoforte every morning before serving her family breakfast. According to her niece Caroline Austen , “Aunt Jane began her day with music.” Austen’s family owned around 600 pieces of music, including works by Mozart, Haydn, and Clementi, so she had plenty to choose from. Music also found its way into her novels, where several characters play the piano, and scholars have noted the musicality imbued into Austen’s prose. Her morning practice also ran against some of the expectations around women and music at the time. The Jane Austen Society of North America notes that piano playing could be viewed as a “frivolous” party trick, meant “only for temporarily attracting the admiration of men.” For Austen, though, it was an everyday part of her morning, right before turning her attention to the social satire and romantic plots that would make her famous. Research into music and creativity suggests there may be something to that idea Studies of musical improvisation have found changes in brain activity in regions involved in conscious self-monitoring, while other research has found that certain kinds of music can improve performance on tasks that measure divergent thinking, or the ability to come up with multiple possible ideas. But you don’t necessarily need to pick up an instrument to give your brain a musical nudge. Music can influence mood and arousal , which can in turn affect creative thinking. In one study , people who listened to upbeat, positive classical music performed better on a measure of divergent thinking than people who worked in silence. That doesn’t mean putting on any random playlist will suddenly turn you into Jane Austen. The research is still limited , and the effects can depend on what’s being listened to, the person listening, and the creative task. But it does give us a reason to experiment with how we use music before we create. Try making music part of your creative warm-up If you’re struggling to get your ideas moving, you could borrow a little inspiration from Austen. Make a playlist for the work. Choose music that puts you in the mood you want to bring to your project. If lyrics pull your attention away from the task, try instrumental music instead. Give yourself a musical runway. Rather than pressing play and immediately diving into your work, spend five or 10 minutes listening while you make coffee, stretch, tidy your workspace, or sitting and meditationg on. The point is to create a small transition between everyday life and creative work. Play something yourself. You don’t need to be a virtuoso. Play piano, guitar, drums, or whatever instrument you have available. You could even sing or hum a simple melody. Use music to change gears. Try keeping different playlists for different kinds of creative work. Something energetic might help when you’re brainstorming, while something calmer could work better when you’re revising or editing. Try a little improvisation. If you play an instrument, spend a few minutes playing without trying to make anything “good.” The goal is to experiment and let your brain wander before you ask it to produce something polished. Find your “Austen” song. Pick one piece of music that you use consistently before a particular creative task. Over time, it may become a cue that tells your brain it’s time to switch gears and start creating. We can’t know exactly what was happening in Austen’s head as she played, or whether she deliberately used music to get herself into a creative flow state. But between what we know about her routine and what researchers are learning about music and creative thinking, there’s a good reason to experiment with the idea ourselves. The post Jane Austen’s daily piano warm-up may hold a surprisingly simple lesson about creativity appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: There are plenty of animals with impressive survival strategies, but sea urchins may have one of the most entertaining ones. Some of them have taken their already unusual appearance a step further by developing a habit that makes them look like they’re wearing tiny hats . Adaptation at its most adorable? We think so. A fun video from BBC Earth shows these creatures picking up shells and other bits of debris and placing them on top of their bodies as they strut across the ocean floor. Sea urchins use thousands of tiny tube feet to move around and interact with objects in their environment. Those same appendages allow them to grab pieces of material from the seafloor and position them over their bodies, creating what looks like a miniature collection of ocean-floor accessories. Aside from providing a delightful dose of underwater whimsy, this behavior has a very practical purpose. More than a bold fashion choice Researchers have been studying this phenomenon for decades, and one major reason sea urchins cover themselves is to protect against UV light. That can be especially important in shallow water, where sunlight is stronger. It may also become more useful as kelp forests decline, since the towering plants often act as a natural canopy for sea urchins and countless other marine animals. There is a complication here, though. Sea urchins eat kelp, and when their populations grow too large, they can contribute to the loss of entire kelp forests. So the animals can help shape the very habitat that provides them with protection. When that canopy disappears, an urchin can’t exactly grab an umbrella and head for the shade. It can, however, pick up a shell. Scientists are still uncovering the reasons behind it Sun protection isn’t necessarily the whole story, either. Researchers have found evidence that covering can provide physical protection as well. A recent study of green sea urchins found that the objects they carry can help shield their bodies from moving debris caused by waves, giving them another reason to keep their improvised headwear close. It’s essentially the ocean’s version of Project Runway’s Unconventional Materials challenge , with the urchins turning whatever they find into functional fashion. Anything can be a hat if you’re creative enough Sea urchins use a wide range of materials, too. They’ve been observed carrying shells, rocks, pieces of algae, and other natural debris. Researchers have even documented them carrying human-made objects, including pieces of plastic , when those materials make themselves available in their environment. Basically, sea urchins appear to appreciate micro-fashion trends just as much as humans, from shellcore to rockcore to whatever-you-can-find-on-the-seafloor-core. Sea urchins have some stylish company Interestingly, sea urchins aren’t the only sea animals getting creative with accessories. Sponge crabs carry pieces of sponge on their backs for camouflage and protection, while decorator crabs attach algae, sponges, and other organisms to their bodies. Even whales have gotten in on the trend. Orcas have sported salmon hats, while humpback whales have been observed balancing pieces of kelp on their heads and bodies, a behavior researchers have nicknamed “kelping,” though they are still figuring out exactly why they do it . Now the real question: Will these aquatic style icons someday have their own Met Gala? The post Sea urchins have a bizarre habit of wearing shells as hats. A fun video shows why they do it. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Actor Charlie Chaplin and actress Sophia Loren developed a strong relationship Chaplin, whose career began in silent film in 1914 , was someone Loren looked up to. So when the legendary actor asked the Italian actress to be in the 1967 film he was directing, A Countess from Hong Kong , she was thrilled. “When Charlie Chaplin asked me to do ( A Countess from Hong Kong , 1967) I was really very, very happy. I would never have thought that he was going to ask me to be the lead in his last film. It was a wonderful relationship between me and Charlie Chaplin,” she told the South China Morning Post . Loren shared in her 2014 memoir Yesterday, Today, Tomorrow: My Life that Chaplin had come into her life in the 1960s. And it was during this time together that Chaplin pointed out a major flaw he saw in Loren. He subsequently offered her advice at 50-years-old that had a profound impact and changed her life. View this post on Instagram Loren and Chaplin’s friendship blossoms Loren recalled her excitement to work with the Hollywood legend. “I was so nervous working with him. He’s such a master. But on the first day on the set, I realized he was just as nervous. If you care and love something, you get nervous. I’m suspicious of people who don’t ever get nervous,” she told The Wrap . She also told The Los Angeles Times , “[Writer-director] Charlie Chaplin wanted me because he saw a picture I did with [Vittorio] De Sica, maybe it was ‘Gold of Naples,’ and he said ‘I want this girl.’ He could have given me the telephone book and I would have done it anyway.” During the film, Loren and Chaplin became close—with Chaplin offering Loren wisdom that she took to heart. Chaplin’s advice for Loren During a 1984 interview on The Merv Griffin Show , Loren recalled a tender moment between her and Chaplin that deeply impacted her. Loren shared that Chaplin told her, “‘There’s one thing that I don’t like about you’,” he told her. She replied, “What is it?” And his brutal honesty struck a chord: “That you always say ‘yes’. You don’t know how to say ‘no’,” she shared. “Then I realized, I said, ‘Maybe this wonderful person is right. I don’t know how to say no.” Loren continued, “I said, ‘This is a terrible failure for a person, because if you don’t know how to say ‘no’, you spend your time in doing things that you don’t want to do. You can’t organize your day. And you can’t do in your day what you wish because you are always at [the] disposal of other people.” Griffin replied, “You never please yourself, right? Constantly pleasing everybody else.” And Loren said, “Mmhmm. But now I do. I’m 50 years old and I learned how to say ‘no’.” In her memoir, Loren expanded on the interaction. Chaplin told her: “‘Sophia, my dear, you have one imperfection which you must overcome if you wish to be a truly happy woman. You have to learn to say ‘No.’ Enough with always trying to please everyone, enough with trying to satisfy everything and everyone. ‘No,’ ‘No,’ and again ‘No.’ You still don’t know how to say that word, and this is a serious drawback. Learning to say ‘No’ is of essential importance to being able to do as you please with your time. It was hard for me, too, but from the moment I got it, nothing was ever the same again: my life became much simpler.'” Loren also added , “Only age can offer you this sense of self-confidence. And only this self-confidence can nourish the beauty within each of us.” The post Charlie Chaplin noticed Sophia Loren’s one major flaw. His simple advice changed her life at 50. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: When you’re hanging out in a low-stakes social situation, like a lazy Sunday barbecue or gabbing with your neighbor while he waters his lawn, it’s easy to fall into the trap of being vague. How often do you hear these types of responses to simple small-talk questions? “How’s it going?” “It’s going.” “What did you do last weekend?” “Nothing, just hung out.” “Did you see the game last night?” “Yeah, total bummer.” Vague answers make you less likable A 2024 study from James Cook University in Singapore, by Dr. Deming (Adam) Wang and his team, found that when people give vague answers, others see them as less likable than those who give full details. The study also found that people are less likely to want to date or befriend someone who gives ambiguous answers. Two people chatting over champagne. Credit: Canva When people give vague answers, even in low-stakes social situations, people think they are trying to conceal something or aren’t interested in interacting with them. Vague people are also judged as being less warm, less extraverted, less gullible, and more cautious. “When asked a question, people often give responses that are not as precise as the questioner had hoped for. Sometimes this vagueness is deliberate, but other times the responder could just be tired, distracted, or genuinely unable to recall the specific answer to a question,” Wang remarked . “Our research reveals the impact of vague responses on likeability. It emphasises the importance of clear communication in daily life, because likeability pulls some serious weight in both our social and professional successes.” Couple drinking beer on a first date. Credit: Canva Many of us probably give vague answers because we don’t think the conversation is that serious and, sometimes, it’s okay to be laid-back. But while this may seem like a decent social strategy, it can unintentionally send the wrong message. “Often times you’ll come across people who are not very social and don’t really want to engage with you, so they’ll brush you off with a perfunctory answer, which can often be ambiguous,” Wang continues . “Conversely, if well-meaning people are unknowingly damaging their reputation by being non-committal, this research may help increase their awareness of these social blind spots.” Women enjoying wine at a party. Credit: Canva How to be more likable? Give a detailed response. Here are some responses to the questions above that aren’t vague and will make you more likable. The answers don’t have to be all that complex, just something that makes it appear that you’re engaged and provide some fodder for the other person’s response “How’s it going?” “Pretty good, I tried cooking a new steak recipe last night, and it turned out great.” “What did you do last weekend?” “We kinda stayed in the house, but I did watch that new Netflix show about vampires.” “Did you see the game last night?” “Yeah, it’s rare for Nix to throw interceptions, so I was shocked when he threw that one on the fourth. The study found a situation where giving a vague response didn’t hurt the person’s likability. That’s when they are seen as trying to “soften the blow,” when they are delivering bad news or want to protect someone’s feelings. Ultimately, when someone strikes up a conversation with you, they want to hear what you have to say or at least interact with someone who doesn’t seem uninterested or being elusive. The good news is that it’s not too hard to be interesting; just share a few more details than you naturally would to show the other person you’re engaged. The post Social psychologist found a simple conversation habit that instantly makes people more likable appeared first on Upworthy .

Αποδείχθηκε ότι ήταν ένα από τα πέντε ξεχασμένα κομμάτια Fabergé, συμπεριλαμβανομένων δύο κορνίζες με χρυσό, που η καθεμία κρατούσε ένα…
items.descriptionOriginal: In 2019, Geoffrey Munn, the jewelry expert from “ Antiques Roadshow ,” was looking through the storerooms of the Brighton Museum & Art Gallery in England when he noticed the corner of a frame poking out of some archival tissue paper. It turned out to be one of five forgotten Fabergé pieces, including two gold-mounted picture frames, each holding a photograph of an elegant woman in furs, lace and pearls. Nobody knew who the women were. Munn and two of the museum’s curators had tried to find out but came up empty. So when the Fabergé pieces went on display in 2021, the museum added a sign asking visitors for help. View this post on Instagram In March 2024, actor and screenwriter Andreane Rellou ( @andreanerellou ), who’s from Athens and based in London, visited the museum with her sister and read it. Then she went home and started digging. “I used my knowledge of historical fashion and hairstyling to try and date the pictures myself,” Rellou told the museum . She guessed the woman in the smaller, square frame was in her early 40s, and her clothes and hair pointed to the early 1900s. And because Fabergé frames have always been expensive, she figured the woman had serious money. View this post on Instagram That meant she had likely married in the 1880s, and she had married well. “At that point, I searched through debutante portraits, and then I looked through lists of recently married men of the upper classes … and the Rothschild name came up,” Rellou told Smithsonian . “I gasped when I came across Marie Perugia’s portrait from the Rothschild Archive website,” she said. Perugia, born in Italy in 1862, had married Leopold de Rothschild, one of the wealthiest men of his era, in 1881. Rellou cracked it in about four hours and emailed the museum the next day. The woman in the diamond-shaped frame took a few more days. Rellou compared her face against portraits of royalty and aristocrats until she found the match: Sophia of Prussia, a granddaughter of Queen Victoria, sister of Germany’s Kaiser Wilhelm II, and Queen of Greece from 1913 to 1917. “We’re extremely happy to have the mystery solved at last,” Paula Wrightson of Brighton & Hove Museums told the Greek newspaper To Vima . Rellou is quick to share credit. “My research very much relied on the work of others, so in a way it feels like a collaborative effort,” she told the museum. “I just put the dots together.” What stuck with her was how completely two once-prominent women had been forgotten. “These women deserve to be remembered,” she said, “and I’m very happy that their names will now be heard and spoken again.” The post Woman’s knowledge of fashion history cracked a 120-year-old Fabergé mystery after a museum visit appeared first on Upworthy .

Αναπτύχθηκε χρησιμοποιώντας τεχνολογία παρόμοια με τα εμβόλια mRNA του COVID-19, οι σταγόνες μύτης διεγείρουν την παραγωγή μιας πρωτεΐνης που προστατεύει τον εγκέφαλο που ενισχύει τους νευρώνες και υποστηρίζει…
items.descriptionOriginal: A revolutionary new nasal treatment has restored youthful learning and memory performance in aging mice while preventing severe cognitive decline in mice with Alzheimer’s-like disease. Developed using technology similar to COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, the nose drops stimulate production of a brain-protecting protein that strengthens neurons and supports memory. Remarkably, the treatment preserved brain function without removing Alzheimer’s-associated plaques, suggesting a completely different way to combat cognitive decline.

items.descriptionOriginal: A laboratory mishap has led German researchers to the unexpected discovery of a potentially cleaner and more efficient way to recover valuable rare earth metals from old electronics, such as wind turbines and smartphones. The breakthrough was made by six researchers from the Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf (HHU), and the Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR). Two of them, Lena Daumann, PhD, a professor of bioinorganic chemistry at HHU, and Sophie Marie Gutenthaler-Tietze, PhD, initially set out to understand how bacteria capture rare earth elements. After accidentally assembling a peptide in reverse order, they left it forgotten in a freezer for several years. When they revisited the experiment, they discovered that peptides with reversed amino acid sequences could bind lanthanides roughly 10 times more strongly than their natural counterparts. The research team believes the findings could lead to cleaner ways to recover and separate rare earth metals, which are hard to extract and process without harming the environment. The discovery has earned the group the Mario Markus Prize for Ludic Sciences from the German Chemical Society (GDCh). A blessing in disguise As part of their initial research, Daumann and Gutenthaler-Tietze reproduced the metal-binding regions of a bacterial protein called lanmodulin. The protein has a high affinity for lanthanides, a group of 15 chemically similar metallic elements. The researchers recreated these sections as peptides, which are short chains of amino acids. However, due to a lack of experience at the time, they accidentally assembled their first peptide in reverse order. After noticing the mistake , the researchers placed the peptide in a freezer, where it remained for several years. Driven by curiosity, they later decided to investigate whether the sequence of amino acids mattered, in case the number and spacing of those responsible for metal binding remained the same. The award-winning team. Credit : Jonathan Gutenthaler-Tietze / Björn Drobot Together with their colleagues at HZDR, Björn Drobot, Jérôme Kretzschmar, Robin Steudtner, and Satoru Tsushima, the researchers examined the previously frozen peptide alongside three other reversed variants, and were stunned by the results. Three of the four reversed peptides bound lanthanides approximately 10 times more strongly than peptides with their natural amino acid sequences. The fourth initially showed no improvement. Still, after replacing a single amino acid , the researchers achieved an exceptionally high metal-binding affinity for a peptide of its length. A new route to rare earths The discovery could make it easier to recover critical raw materials. The 17 rare earth elements are widely utilized in technologies including smartphones, wind turbines, batteries, and defense or medical equipment. According to the researchers, the findings could lead to peptides that can capture and separate specific lanthanides. Still, the team is yet to determine whether these molecules can, in fact, be used in practical recycling processes. The German Chemical Society praised the study for its originality, scientific merit, and playful approach to research. The six researchers will be presented with the award on December 15 in Frankfurt, Germany, where they will also share their findings. “The team will receive a EUR 10,000 [USD 11,000] prize for a discovery made possible by a laboratory error,” the German Chemical Society (GDCh) said in a press release . The study has been published in the journal Angewandte Chemie International Edition .

items.description: Ερευνητές στις ΗΠΑ μόλις παρουσίασαν ένα μοντέλο πρόβλεψης εμπνευσμένο από φυσικά κοχύλια, που θα μπορούσε να διευκολύνει την παραγωγή σκληρών συνθετικών υλικών σε νανοκλίμακα. Το έργο συγκέντρωσε ερευνητές από το Εθνικό Εργαστήριο Βορειοδυτικού Ειρηνικού (PNNL) του Υπουργείου Ενέργειας των ΗΠΑ και το Πανεπιστήμιο Cornell. Η ομάδα ανέπτυξε ένα προγνωστικό μ…
items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers in the US have just unveiled a predictive model inspired by natural seashells, that could make it easier to produce tough synthetic materials at the nanoscale. The project brought together researchers from the US Department of Energy’s Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL) and Cornell University. The team developed a predictive model for building structures that mimic biomaterials, such as seashells. The model could show how to incorporate nanomaterials into growing crystals based on their surface chemistry. The structures examined in the study form at the nanoscale, roughly 10,000 times smaller than the width of a human hair. To understand how they form, the team combined chemical theory with specialized instruments that can track changes at the atomic level. Elias Nakouzi, PhD, a materials scientist at PNNL and one of the project leaders, said the team confirmed the model’s predictions through lab experiments. “The model made predictions, and then we went out and did the experiments, and sure enough, the experiment panned out the way we predicted,” he disclosed. Nature’ toughest materials Scientists have attempted to mimic how marine organisms build tough shells for common minerals, for decades. Still, replicating these structure in the laboratory has proven difficult. Seashells are created through biomineralization, a natural process in which living organisms produce minerals to build hard structures like shells, bones and teeth. The team examined how nanoparticles interact with growing crystals of calcite, a form of calcium carbonate. The mineral is found in chalk and marine shells. The team initially attempted to predict how nanoparticles would behave based on their surface chemistry. But this only partly explained the findings. The group then found that the energy needed for nanoparticles to penetrate the organized layers of water molecules at the crystal surface was another important factor. Once the team incorporated this factor into their model , its predictions matched their experimental observations. “Our excitement comes from discovering a new understanding and design rules at the most fundamental level,” Nakouzi said. A new approach To examine the interactions, the team relied on three-dimensional atomic force microscopy ( 3D-AFM ). The technique can measure interactions between liquids and solid surfaces at the molecular level. According to Nakouzi, it exists in fewer than 10 laboratories worldwide. The researchers coated a tiny probe with the same molecules used to modify the surface chemistry of their nanoparticles. This enabled them to measure the forces that nanoparticles would encounter as they neared a crystal surface surrounded by water molecules and ions. “In a way, we can use the probe to ‘feel’ the environment from the nanoparticle’s perspective,” Mingyi Zhang, PhD, a professor at the University of Oklahoma, and first author of the study, pointed out in a press release . She said that many of the processes involved in material formation occur at scales too small to observe. Zhang highlighted that the experimental approach made it possible to recreate conditions similar to those found in natural aquatic environments and examine how individual building blocks interact. The findings could provide a framework for the development of synthetic materials that incorporate nanoparticles into crystalline structures. The study has been published in the journal Science Advances .

items.descriptionOriginal: Το μεγαλύτερο εργοστάσιο δορυφόρων της Ευρώπης εγκαινιάστηκε χθες, Τρίτη (24/11) στη βελγική πόλη Σαρλερουά για να καλύψει, μεταξύ άλλων, τη ζήτηση για το μελλοντικό ευρωπαϊκό σύστημα δορυφόρων Iris², το οποίο στοχεύει στην ενίσχυση της διαστημικής αυτονομίας της Γηραιάς Ηπείρου. «Εξελιχθήκαμε από μια πολύ μικρή εταιρεία» το 2018 «σε ένα σχέδιο μεγάλης εμβέλειας, σημαντικό για την Ευρώπη και την διαστημική της κυριαρχία», δήλωσε ο διευθύνων σύμβουλος της Aerospacelab Μπενουά Ντεπέρ, εγκαινιάζοντας το «μεγα-εργοστάσιο» παρουσία του βασιλιά του Βελγίου. Με δυνατότητα παραγωγής περίπου 500 δορυφόρων ετησίως, αυτό το εργοστάσιο θα είναι το μεγαλύτερο στην Ευρώπη και ένα από τα μεγαλύτερα στον κόσμο, είπε σε ΜΜΕ. Γεννημένος στο Σαρλερουά, ο Ντεπέρ βελτίωσε τις δεξιότητές του στη NASA πριν επιστρέψει στο Βέλγιο για να ξεκινήσει την Aerospacelab το 2018. Οκτώ χρόνια αργότερα, στα 40 του, επέστρεψε στην πόλη του, το όνομα της οποίας παραπέμπει περισσότερο σε υποβαθμισμένους βιομηχανικούς χώρους και εγκαταλελειμμένα εργοστάσια παρά σε υψηλή τεχνολογία. Κι όμως, το Σαρλερουά έχει «μια κουλτούρα διαστημικής μηχανικής», ισχυρίζεται. Η Thales Alenia Space, ένας σημαντικός παράγοντας στον ευρωπαϊκό διαστημικό τομέα, επέλεξε να εγκαταστήσει την έδρα της στο Βέλγιο, μια χώρα που «ανθίζει στον διαστημικό τομέα», σύμφωνα με την υπουργό Εκσυγχρονισμού του Βελγίου Βανέσα Ματζ. «Μεγα-εργοστάσιο» Το 2022, η Aerospacelab δεν είχε μεγαλεπήβολα σχέδια όταν άνοιξε την πρώτη της μονάδα παραγωγής στη Λουβέν-Λα-Νεβ, κοντά στις Βρυξέλλες, με δυνατότητα παραγωγής μόνο 25 δορυφόρων. «Δεν θέλαμε να κάνουμε το ίδιο λάθος» και ελήφθη η απόφαση να κατασκευαστεί ένα «μεγα-εργοστάσιο», ένα τεράστιο οβάλ κτίριο από μέταλλο και ατσάλι που εκτείνεται σε περίπου 20.000 τετραγωνικά μέτρα, του οποίου ο θεμέλιος λίθος τέθηκε στις 16 Μαΐου. Αυτό ήταν ακόμη πιο κρίσιμο δεδομένου ότι ο Μπενουά Ντεπέρ και οι συνεργάτες του εξασφάλισαν μια σύμβαση 2,4 δισεκατομμυρίων ευρώ τον Σεπτέμβριο για την παραγωγή 264 από τους 348 δορυφόρους που είχαν προγραμματιστεί για το σύστημα δορυφόρων Iris². Αυτοί οι δορυφόροι χαμηλής και μέσης τροχιάς θα επιτρέψουν στην Ευρώπη, έως το 2030, να έχει το δικό της ασφαλές τηλεπικοινωνιακό δίκτυο, αμφισβητώντας την κυριαρχία του Starlink του Ίλον Μασκ. «Έχουμε αναπτυχθεί ταχύτερα από τις φιλοδοξίες μας, χάρη στους πελάτες και τους εταίρους μας», τόνισε ο επικεφαλής της Aerospacelab. Εν τω μεταξύ, οι τεράστιοι «αποστειρωμένο χώροι», όπου δεκάδες μηχανικοί θα εργάζονται σε μια εντελώς καθαρή ατμόσφαιρα από το επόμενο έτος, είναι ακόμα άδειοι. «Οι ομάδες θα μετακινηθούν όλες τον Ιανουάριο, ενόψει της προγραμματισμένης έναρξης της παραγωγής στα τέλη του 2028», επιβεβαίωσε ο Μισέλ Μαρισάλ, επικεφαλής επιχειρήσεων της Aerospacelab. Και για να σηματοδοτήσει αυτό το νέο ξεκίνημα, η εταιρεία θα αλλάξει το όνομά της. Από τον Δεκέμβριο, θα ονομάζεται Ectro, μια ονομασία που επινόησε ο Μπενουά Ντεπέρ. Πηγές: ΑΠΕ-ΜΠΕ, AFP www.ertnews.gr

items.description: Αν έχετε την ευκαιρία να δείτε το Wildwood στη μεγάλη οθόνη, κάντε το οπωσδήποτε. Αλλά συνιστώ ανεπιφύλακτα να βουτήξετε στη δημιουργία της ταινίας πριν πάτε, αντί για μετά. Υπόσχομαι ότι δεν θα καταστρέψετε καμία από τις κινηματογραφικές μαγείες κοιτάζοντας πρώτα πίσω από την κουρτίνα. Στην πραγματικότητα, δεν μπορείτε να εκτιμήσετε πλήρως πόσο μαγικό είναι πραγματικά αν δεν πάρετε μια γεύση του γιατί…
items.descriptionOriginal: If you have the chance to see Wildwood on the big screen , definitely do it. But I highly recommend diving into the making of the film before you go, instead of after. I promise, you won’t ruin any of the movie magic by peeking behind the curtain first. In fact, you can’t fully appreciate how magical it truly is unless you get a glimpse of why it took 16 years to plan and create it. Wildwood is like no animated film you’ve ever seen If you’ve seen Laika Studios’ other films (such as Coraline , ParaNorman , Kubo and the Two Strings ) and understand how they were made, you might be able to appreciate Wildwood for what it is. But even at that, Laika has never done a stop-motion film on the scale of Wildwood , and neither has anyone else. When I say there aren’t enough adjectives to describe how mind-blowing it is, I’m being literal. It’s not that the story itself is outstanding; it’s based on a fantasy book series and has the elements you’d expect. But the artistry that went into telling that story and the layers of human creativity beneath it deserve all the accolades, because WOW . 16,000 handmade feathers for just one character Laika Studios creates elaborate handmade sets for all of its films, paying attention to the tiniest of details. And in Wildwood , there are a lot—like a lot —of details. For intance, a golden eagle named The General, who helps the main character, Prue, was created with 16,000 individual, handmade feathers across several different puppets. And that was just one bird. This film is full of birds, in addition to humans, coyotes, and more. Laika chief marketing & operations officer Dave Burke told Variety that the studio likes to always top its previous work. For Wildwood , that meant an incredibly ambitious scope. “We’ve got 136 locations in the feature, and many of them are so large that the crew can walk through them,” he said. “We’ve really moved from that tabletop world into a grand, sweeping, kind of mythical epic. … There’s 231 practical puppets, 54 hero characters, and each and every one of them has been engineered and costumed like a bespoke work of art.” Characters had to change their facial expressions in nearly every frame of the film. At 24 frames per second , that meant making over 140,000 individual 3D-printed faces, each one just slightly different. The scale of everything they created for this 2 hour and 20 minute film is truly jaw-dropping. A beautiful ‘love letter to Portland’ Travis Knight, CEO of Laika and director of Wildwood , has called the film his “love letter to Portland.” Knight is the son of Phil Knight, the founder of Nike, and has lived in the Portland area almost his entire life. As someone who loves Portland, this film feels like a love letter to the area. The natural wilderness woven throughout the city, the quirky people, the iconic Powell’s bookstore, Pittock Mansion, and more are showcased in beautiful detail. There’s even a cameo by the UniPiper, a Darth Vader mask-wearing unicycler who rides around Portland playing the bagpipes. (Yes, he’s a real person .) Prue’s parents are quintessential Portland hipsters. I giggled out loud when, after watching the film in a Portland suburb, I saw a couple who looked exactly like them at the grocery store that same evening. If you know Portland at all, it will feel familiar. If you’ve never been, you might wonder if the portrayal is accurate. To me, as someone who visits frequently, it really does feel as magical as the film. An artistic labor of love funded by Nike’s success Travis Knight is a billionaire, thanks to the shares he holds in Nike. He certainly hasn’t become wealthy from running Laika Studios. In fact, most of the studio’s films lose money. Coraline is the only one of Laika’s six feature films that has outearned its budget. But Knight keeps making movies anyway, funded from his own family’s pocket. Wildwood reportedly had a $100 million budget. According to the Motion Picture Association , Knight employed more than 1,000 artists, craftspeople, technicians, and filmmakers, including 49 animators in the making of the film. Wildwood hasn’t even come close to recouping that cost at the box office. It doesn’t matter. Funding of the arts by the wealthy is a long-standing tradition, and in the age of AI, supporting genuine, human-created art feels like a pretty worthwhile investment. A celebration of human artistry and creativity When you’ve seen what happened behind the scenes to make Wildwood , it’s easy to see it as a celebration of art and artistry. But Laika doesn’t shun technology altogether. “We do use computers; we’re not Amish,” Knight told a live audience at the Academy of Motional Pictures Museum. “We’re not making these things by candlelight while we’re churning butter in the background, using tools from a watchmaker’s widow.” Wildwood includes some CGI animation when necessary. But Knight says they draw the line at AI. “It’s incredible technology,” he told Thomas Duke . “But there’s no humanity to it.” Even digital animation has a human artist behind it, and Knight intentionally makes sure every part of a Laika film is “brought to life by an artist’s hands.” The end credits are delightful, and include a listing of the first names of "Wildwood Babies" born to cast and crew members during the 15 year journey of making of this film… https://t.co/N7ebNCCrFF — Peg Aloi (@themediawitch) October 24, 2026 Wildwood is definitely worth seeing on as large a screen as possible to really appreciate all the details. If you do see it in a theater, stay through the credits to see the list the names of more than 80 babies born to the cast and crew during the production of the film—a testament not only to the years that went into it, but to the humans behind it as well. The post There aren’t enough adjectives to describe how mind-blowing the making of ‘Wildwood’ actually was appeared first on Upworthy .

items.titleOriginal: The man who wrote the Carpenters’ bank jingle also gave a frog his signature song
items.description: Ο μουσικός και συνθέτης Paul Williams ήταν πολύ απασχολημένος τη δεκαετία του 1970 . Δεν έγραφε μόνο υπέροχα τραγούδια επιτυχιών, αλλά και πραγματικά διάσημοι άνθρωποι το πρόσεχαν. Οι David Bowie, οι Carpenters, οι Three Dog Night, η Helen Reddy και ακόμη και ο Jim Henson (της φήμης των Muppets) του βοήθησαν να κερδίσει πολλές διακρίσεις που τους άξιζε. Σε μια συνέντευξη podcast στο Smashing Pum…
items.descriptionOriginal: Musician and composer Paul Williams was very busy in the 1970s . He was not only writing brilliant hit songs, but truly famous people were taking note. The likes of David Bowie, the Carpenters, Three Dog Night, Helen Reddy and even Jim Henson (of the Muppets fame) helped get him many well-deserved accolades. In a podcast interview with Smashing Pumpkins lead singer Billy Corgan, Williams explains how his career esculated. “Roger (Nichols) and I were writing all these songs. And we had met the Carpenters . Incidentally, Roger and I were getting all these cuts. And nothing was ever on the radio. I mean, album cuts, B-sides. Nothing on there. I mean, nobody knew who we were. There was no real chart success, but we were making a great living. B-sides! I mean, I wrote the B-sides of ‘I Am Woman’ and ‘Delta Dawn.’” Meet the Carpenters He continues, “So all of a sudden, there’s a knock at the door in Roger’s office, and it’s Chuck Kaye and Herb Alpert and they said, ‘This is our newest act at A&M (records). Wanted you to meet Karen and Richard Carpenter.’ And they looked at Roger and I were like, ‘Oh man, we love your Peppermint Trolley cut of ‘Trust’ and the Steve Lawrence recording of ‘Drifter.’ And we’re like, ‘We’re famous, oh my God.’ We’re so excited because these two kids knew who we were. Williams shares how exciting things got. “When they recorded ‘Close to You,’ which was their first huge hit, the B-side was ‘I Kept on Loving You,’ that Roger and I wrote. It was going to be the A-side, but they turned it over and played ‘Close to You’ because was a major, major free ride.” Things took a turn. “But then what happened was Tony Asher, a wonderful songwriter, was supposed to write a commercial for Crocker Bank, and he had a skiing accident. He broke his hand, so he suggested Roger and I write a little song, not a pitch, just a little video of a wedding. Show a young couple getting married and at the end say, ‘You’ve got a long way to go, we’d like to help you get there. The Crocker Bank.’ Life changing Williams didn’t particularly want to write a bank commercial. “I said to Roger, ‘I don’t want to write a bank commercial! I’m street. I’m white lightning and black leather.’ He said, well, there’s a creative fee. So we wrote this in an afternoon, wrote the song. And I sang it on the commercial, and he did the background voices. …Richard Carpenter heard it in the commercial and said, ‘Is there a full song?’ And I said, ‘We’ve Only Just Begun,’ and that changed our lives.” While Williams was already a proficient talent, “only just begun” was a perfect way to describe what came next. Alongside Kenneth Ascher (with whom he often co-wrote), Williams already had a working relationship/friendship with Jim Henson, creator of The Muppets. So when they were asked to write songs for the The Muppet Movie , Williams was already a fan. He’s a frog with rainbows In an interview with the Bluegrass Situation , Williams shares some of the difficulty he had when tasked to write a song for Kermit. “The big thing with that song was that we had to show that Kermit has an inner life. The song that Kenny and I tried to shoot for was ‘When You Wish Upon a Star.’ When Jiminy Cricket sings that song, it’s so touching. There’s so much depth there. We wanted to do something like that with Kermit. He’s a frog. He’s got water. He’s got refracted light. So he’s got rainbows. That seemed like the obvious thing for us to write about.” But there was an issue. Williams continues, “But we quickly wrote ourselves into the worst corner. ‘Why are there so many songs about rainbows? What’s on the other side? Rainbows are visions, but only illusions. Rainbows have nothing to hide.’ Oh, shit, look what we did! We painted ourselves into a corner. We’re advocating for people to grow up and knock off all that dreamy rainbow crap.” When asked how he got around it, Williams admits, “I don’t know what happened, but we managed to follow it up with ‘So we’ve been told and some choose to believe it. I know they’re wrong. Wait and see. Someday we’ll find it, the rainbow connection, the lovers, the dreamers, and me.’ In that moment, Kermit ceases to be this creature, this Yoda or mentor or whatever, and he becomes a member of the audience. He becomes part of the public that is affected by this magic. So that was a gift.” Full circle Everything in this magical songwriting universe seemed to have come full circle. In the early 80s, Karen Carpenter recorded her own version of “The Rainbow Connection.” On Richard Carpenter’s site, he shares that their version was released as outtakes on their Made in America album. It wouldn’t be until decades later that Richard would release the full version. The post The man who wrote the Carpenters’ bank jingle also gave a frog his signature song appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Ο φίλος της CIA του Ρόμπερτ Ντε Νίρο μοιράστηκε ένα «άβολο» μέρος της εκπαίδευσής του. Ο ηθοποιός το μετέτρεψε στη σκηνή που έκανε το «Meet the Parents».
items.titleOriginal: Robert De Niro’s CIA buddy shared an ‘uncomfortable’ part of his training. The actor turned it into the scene that made ‘Meet the Parents.’
items.description: Μερικές κινηματογραφικές στιγμές είναι τόσο ουσιαστικά τέλειες, που προορίζονται να γίνουν κλασικές από το πρώτο καρέ. Η σκηνή του ανιχνευτή ψεύδους στο Meet the Parents είναι μία από αυτές. Μόνο που δεν υπήρχε σχεδόν ποτέ. Με το Focker-In-Law να έρχεται σύντομα, το cringe-and-comedy franchise επιστρέφει στους κινηματογράφους. Αλλά η χαρακτηριστική σκηνή που μας έκανε όλους να ταρακουνηθεί…
items.descriptionOriginal: Some movie moments are so quintessentially perfect , they’re destined to become a classic from the opening frame . The lie detector scene in Meet the Parents is one of them. Except it almost never existed at all. With Focker-In-Law arriving soon , the cringe-and-comedy franchise is returning to theaters. But the signature scene that had us all shaking with laughter more than 25 years ago wasn’t in the original screenplay. You know the moment. Robert De Niro plays Jack Byrnes, a suspicious dad who happens to be ex-CIA. When he catches his daughter’s fiancé snooping around his basement, he hooks him up to a polygraph machine. Then starts asking questions that Ben Stiller’s Greg Focker has no idea how to answer. Greg’s anxious sweating and fidgeting comically causes the polygraph needle to jump all over the place, leaving his future father-in-law to wonder: is Greg a truthful man worthy of marrying his daughter? Does he deserve to be in his family’s “circle of trust”? The scene is a perfect blend of high discomfort and big laughs, but where did it come from? A friend, a confession, and a bad day at work De Niro had already met some real-life CIA contacts while doing research for a future role. They shared personal stories with him about their agency training days. One element stood out to the actor as particularly intriguing: the polygraph test. De Niro says his CIA buddies described the process as deeply uncomfortable, invasive, and tense. It was the kind of experience he felt would stay with a person long after the questions stop. The conversation stuck with De Niro, but he had no idea where it would one day pay off. Not until he discussed it with Meet the Parents director Jay Roach. Meeting your partner’s parents is already stressful enough, especially if one of them is a former government agent. De Niro figured his deeply suspicious dad character would want to be sure about Stiller’s Greg. He suggested the idea of hooking Focker up to a polygraph machine to prompt greater honesty. Roach, Stiller, and the creative team loved the notion and scripted out a new scene based on De Niro’s proposal. The results were so iconic, it became the movie’s poster image. The line that milked the audience for even more laughs De Niro’s contributions to Meet the Parents were far from over, however. During camera rehearsals for the first family meal in the film, everyone was riffing around the table. But it was De Niro’s improvised response that stunned the room. After Stiller’s Greg gets backed into a corner about being able to milk anything with nipples, Jack fires back with the perfect response: “I have nipples, Greg. Could you milk me?” It caught the cast and crew completely off guard. In the best way possible. They filmed the scene with the improvised line, and it became pop culture history. A franchise that kept growing Plenty of comedies don’t age very well but the staying power of Meet the Parents is remarkable. Now, another chapter is arriving, adding young stars like Ariana Grande and Beanie Feldstein. And with new co-stars comes the comparison that will have you checking your calendar and your scalp for grey hairs. Ben Stiller is now four years older than De Niro was when they filmed the original in 2000. Back then, Stiller played the anxious young man chasing approval. Now, as the franchise rolls on, he’s finally the one with the power to grant it. The post Robert De Niro’s CIA buddy shared an ‘uncomfortable’ part of his training. The actor turned it into the scene that made ‘Meet the Parents.’ appeared first on Upworthy .

Από την αυτοκρατορία Motown του Ντιτρόιτ μέχρι το folk-rock e…
items.descriptionOriginal: Alt Subhed: Mike Nesmith was told no one would watch music on TV. He proved them wrong. Alt Subhed: Music fans never saw Mike Nesmith’s second act coming, let alone his third. Between the British Invasion and the birth of Flower Power, pop music was constantly transforming during the Swinging Sixties. From Detroit’s Motown empire to the folk-rock evolution, new sounds could pop up anywhere. Even television . In the late 1960s, Michael Nesmith became a household name . He was the sarcastic, wool-hat-wearing member of The Monkees . Together with his bandmates, he starred in the band’s popular NBC television sitcom of the same name. For many artists, being in the “Prefab Four” might be the absolute peak of their career. But for Nesmith, being a Monkee was just the first chapter of a much larger story. Beneath Nesmith’s laconic, twang-infused persona lived a relentless visionary. Turns out it runs in the family. In his autobiography, Infinite Tuesdays , he attributed his inquisitive mind to his mother. Bette Nesmith Graham, you see, invented Liquid Paper . And while Michael grew up comfortable, he yearned more than anything to make music. NBC cancelled The Monkees sitcom after 58 episodes, but Nesmith’s artistic journey was just beginning. He co-wrote the script for The Monkees cult-classic film, “Head.” His collaborator on the story was none other than actor Jack Nicholson . And after the band’s breakup, Nesmith started a journey that fundamentally changed how people consume music and media. The accidental birth of the modern music video In the late 1970s, Nesmith recorded a catchy, breezy solo track titled “Rio.” His record label approached him with a specific request. They needed a promotional clip they could easily ship overseas to broadcast on European television shows. These pre-recorded films were typically cheaper to produce than flying someone across the Atlantic. But in 1977, music videos simply did not exist in the way we know them today. The promo clips tended to be static and unimaginative. So Nesmith took the label’s modest budget and decided to experiment. He hired a small crew and shot a series of whimsical, edited visual vignettes to accompany the song. The concept of pairing popular music with cinematic imagery felt familiar to Nesmith, since songs were performed this way on every episode of The Monkees. His resulting short film for ‘Rio’ felt new and exciting. He didn’t want to just send it overseas for a one-off promo; he wanted to create a new form of music television. Nesmith originally pitched his concept to local TV station executives. He was hoping to start local, then build to national syndication. The television establishment’s reaction was dismissive. In his autobiography, he states their response amounted to, “No one will ever watch music on television.” PopClips goes the world That same year, Nesmith travelled to Australia to promote “Rio.” Local fans couldn’t stop praising what they referred to as his “Pop clip.” That was the colloquial term for music promotional clips Down Under. Michael felt it was the perfect moniker to sell the idea to music and TV execs alike. In 1980, Nesmith produced eight episodes of the show PopClips. The shows were hosted by a “video jockey,” and began airing on a fledgling cable network. You know it now as Nickelodeon. Viewers tuned in by the thousands, proving the cynical executives wrong. PopClips became an instant cultural sensation. New videos were swapped in, especially from artists from the UK. The format of PopClips laid the groundwork for the next stage in music video evolution: a channel of its own. Nesmith was asked to join the core team that would head up the launch of MTV. He ultimately declined the offer. What had intrigued him most was the filmmaking aspect of music videos. He also feared that a corporate TV gig would keep him from making music. His pioneering work in visual media was far from finished, however. His studio, Pacific Arts Corporation, became a leader in independent video distribution and production. Nesmith produced the cult classic Repo Man and directed the comedy title Tapeheads . Set in the early era of music videos, the film stars 80s icons John Cusack and Tim Robbins. A third act that changed technology forever Decades after helping launch the music video revolution, Nesmith secured a completely unexpected third act in the tech world. In 2012, the former Monkee earned an official United States patent for inventing a groundbreaking method to embed live-streaming video directly into a website or virtual environment. Long before streaming video became the backbone of the internet, Nesmith was already sketching out the future. From his first bubblegum pop records to the birth of MTV and early web video architecture, Mike Nesmith proved he was never just a prefabricated television star. He was a genuine technological pioneer who spent his entire life looking over the horizon. The post A Monkee wanted to show people his new song. The film he made pointed toward the future of MTV. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Austin Energy Rebates and Grid Strain Affect What Homeowners Pay to Cool Their Homes, and How to Qualify for Rebates Reading Time: 4 minutes How Austin Energy Rebates and Grid Strain Affect What Homeowners Pay to Cool Their Homes, and How to Qualify for Rebates On a hot Austin afternoon, the room with the west-facing windows can feel like a different house. The thermostat may read 76°F in the hallway while the air conditioner runs steadily and the room still feels warm. That familiar problem connects three things homeowners can act on: how much heat gets indoors, how much electricity it takes to remove it, and what happens when thousands of air conditioners are running at the same time. Austin’s municipal utility offers rebates for qualifying cooling equipment and improvements such as attic insulation and duct sealing. During a heat wave, longer AC run times can raise the monthly electric bill, while a qualifying Austin Energy rebate can lower the upfront cost of an upgrade that helps the home stay cool with less electricity. Where to start depends on what is driving the cooling load in the first place. What Grid Strain Means for an Austin Electric Bill During a stretch of extreme heat, air conditioners run longer across much of Texas. That raises demand on the grid managed by the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, or ERCOT. For most Austin Energy households, the immediate effect on the bill comes from using more kilowatt-hours. The utility’s standard residential energy charge has four usage tiers, so electricity used above a monthly threshold is billed at the higher rate for that tier. A heat wave can increase the bill both by extending AC run times and by pushing some of that extra usage into a higher tier. Wholesale power costs can also affect what households pay over time through Austin Energy’s Power Supply Adjustment. This per-kilowatt-hour charge reflects costs such as fuel and electricity bought from the grid. The standard residential bill uses monthly consumption and published rates, so hourly wholesale price spikes affect households indirectly through the utility’s power supply costs. On your own bill, start by comparing kilowatt-hours with the same billing period last year. The dollar total alone makes it harder to tell how much of the change came from electricity use. Which Cooling Rebate Fits the Work Your Home Needs? When an older system is nearing replacement, Eco Air Conditioning’s guide to Austin Energy rebates ⁠ explains how efficient AC equipment and heat pumps can help reduce cooling demand during periods of grid strain. Austin Energy’s published standalone incentive table lists $600 to $800 for qualifying central split or mini-split AC systems and $650 to $950 for qualifying heat pumps, depending on the equipment and efficiency ratings. Ask the contractor to identify the rebate tier for the exact system on the estimate so you can compare the installed price after the expected rebate. If the old system still works but some rooms are consistently hotter than others, a home energy assessment can help identify where the house is gaining heat or losing cooled air. Austin Energy’s Home Energy Savings program takes this broader approach. A participating contractor conducts a no-cost assessment, and the program requires at least three qualifying improvements. The work may include air and duct sealing, attic insulation or solar screens for eligible windows. A replacement system can also be part of the project when it meets the program’s requirements. How to Qualify Before You Commit to an Installation For the standalone equipment rebate, the home must receive electricity from Austin Energy, and both the home and the system being replaced must be at least 10 years old. The program covers replacements, and the existing equipment must not have received an Austin Energy rebate within the past 10 years. A participating contractor must install a qualifying system. Before signing, have the contractor confirm that the proposed equipment meets the applicable efficiency requirements and that the quote covers the system components required by the program. The contractor must document that the equipment was sized for the home and submit the rebate application within 90 days of installation. The homeowner must also agree to a post-installation inspection. Keep an itemized invoice and ask for the application confirmation so you can track its status. For households looking for help with insulation or duct repairs, Austin Energy also offers a separate Weatherization Assistance program that provides eligible customers with home efficiency improvements at no cost. Shade and Insulation Help Before the AC Switches On The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency ⁠ explains that trees and other vegetation can cool urban areas and reduce air-conditioning demand by shading buildings. At home, that can start with noticing which windows take the strongest afternoon sun. An exterior screen can reduce solar heat gain at a window, while a well-placed tree can provide shade as it grows. Insulation slows heat transfer through the attic, and sealed ducts help cooled air reach the rooms it was meant for. The environmental benefit extends beyond any one property. When homes gain less heat, they need less electricity to stay comfortable. Across a neighborhood, those savings can help ease peak demand on hot afternoons. They can also reduce greenhouse gas emissions when the electricity saved would otherwise have come from fossil fuels. Shade adds a benefit outside the house, too, by helping cool the spaces around buildings. Use Last Summer’s Bills to Decide Where to Start Pull up a few bills from the hottest months and note which rooms were hard to keep cool. Bring both observations to the contractor. If the equipment is nearing the end of its life, compare qualifying replacements by their installed price after the rebate and ask how much electricity the contractor expects each system to use under similar conditions. If the system still runs well, an assessment can help you decide whether insulation, duct repairs or shading would address the discomfort first. Either way, the aim is a home that stays comfortable through the hottest part of the day with less electricity. The post How Austin Energy Rebates and Grid Strain Affect What Homeowners Pay to Cool Their Homes, and How to Qualify for Rebates appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Home Solar Batteries Work, What They Cost and How They Add Resilience During Outages Reading Time: 3 minutes How Home Solar Batteries Work, What They Cost and How They Add Resilience During Outages Rooftop solar panels have become a familiar sight, but more homeowners are now asking a second question: what happens to all that solar energy when the sun goes down, or when the power goes out? Home batteries are the answer for a growing number of households. They store electricity for later use, help homeowners use more of their own clean energy and keep essential appliances running during outages. Here is how home solar batteries work, what affects their cost and why they are becoming an important part of a more resilient, sustainable home. How a Solar Battery System Works Solar panels produce direct current electricity when sunlight hits them. An inverter converts that power into alternating current, which is what household appliances use. During the day, the home uses solar power first. Without a battery, any extra electricity is usually sent back to the grid. With home solar batteries , that extra daytime energy is stored instead. After sunset, or on cloudy days, the battery supplies stored power through the inverter to run lights, appliances and electronics, and in some setups it can even help fcharge an electric vehicle. Batteries can also be charged from the grid, which is useful for homes without solar or for utility programs that reward shifting electricity use away from peak hours. Backup Power When the Grid Goes Down Resilience is one of the main reasons homeowners install batteries. When the grid fails, a properly configured system detects the outage and switches to stored energy automatically, often so quickly that lights barely flicker. The refrigerator keeps running, phones and laptops stay charged and lights stay on. Most residential batteries are designed to power essential circuits rather than an entire home indefinitely. During installation, homeowners usually choose which loads are connected, such as the fridge, internet router, some lighting, a well pump or a furnace fan. With solar panels recharging the battery during the day, a home can keep critical systems running through longer outages. This kind of resilience is increasingly valuable as storms, wildfires and extreme weather put more pressure on electricity grids. An Environmental Win Home batteries also support a cleaner energy system. By storing solar energy produced during the day and using it in the evening, households rely less on electricity generated during peak hours, which in many regions is when fossil fuel power plants are most likely to run. Utilities can also use networks of home batteries to balance demand on the grid, reducing the need to build new peaking power plants. For homeowners, a battery means using more of the clean energy their own roof produces instead of exporting it and buying power back later. Combined with energy efficiency upgrades and electrified heating and transportation, solar and storage help shrink a household’s carbon footprint and support the wider transition to renewable energy. What Home Batteries Cost Battery costs vary widely depending on the size of the battery, the brand, the installation complexity and whether solar panels are installed at the same time. In British Columbia, BC Hydro estimates that the average cost of a lithium-ion solar battery system and installation ranges from about $18,000 to $25,000 for a residential home. Capacity is the biggest factor. Batteries are measured in kilowatt-hours, and a larger battery can power more circuits for longer. Some homes add electrical upgrades, such as a new panel or a dedicated backup sub-panel, which also affect the price. Rebates and Incentives Incentives can reduce the upfront cost. In British Columbia, BC Hydro offers rebates for eligible solar panels and battery storage systems. Residential battery rebates are available, with higher amounts of up to $5,000 for batteries enrolled in its Peak Saver program, which lets the utility draw on stored energy at times of high demand. Solar panel installations may qualify for a separate rebate of up to $5,000. Program rules, eligible products and contractor requirements change from time to time, so it is worth checking current details before buying. Other provinces and states offer their own incentives, and some utilities provide reduced rates or credits for customers who let them use battery capacity during peak periods. Is a Battery Right for You A battery makes the most sense for homes that already have or plan to install solar panels, experience frequent outages, rely on electricity for heating or medical equipment, or want to maximize their use of renewable energy. Homeowners should consider how much backup power they need, which circuits matter most and how long they would like to stay powered during an outage. A qualified installer can review your electricity use, roof and electrical panel, recommend an appropriate battery size and help with permits and rebate applications. Learn More Natural Resources Canada offers information on renewable energy, home energy efficiency and programs that can help Canadians reduce their energy use. Powering a More Resilient Future Home solar batteries turn rooftop panels into a more complete energy system. They store clean power, keep essential appliances running during outages and help support a greener grid. With falling technology costs and available incentives, more homeowners are finding that a battery is a practical step toward both resilience and sustainability. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Common Contaminants in Private Well Water, How to Test for Them and How Treatment Protects Health Reading Time: 3 minutes Common Contaminants in Private Well Water, How to Test for Them and How Treatment Protects Health. For millions of rural households, the tap is connected not to a municipal system but to a private well. Well water can be clean, fresh and reliable, but it comes with a responsibility city residents rarely think about. No utility tests it, treats it or monitors it. That job belongs to the owner. Many contaminants have no taste, smell or colour, so water that looks perfect can still carry health risks. Knowing what to watch for, how to test and how treatment works helps keep families safe. Why Well Water Needs Attention Groundwater moves through soil and rock, picking up minerals and, sometimes, contaminants along the way. Activities on the surface, such as farming, septic systems, roads and industry, can affect water quality. Changes such as flooding, drought or nearby construction can shift conditions underground. Because of this, a well that tested clean years ago is not guaranteed to stay that way, and knowing the most common well water contaminants helps owners decide what to test for. Bacteria Bacteria are among the most common concerns. Total coliform bacteria indicate that surface water or soil may be entering the well, while E. coli points to contamination from human or animal waste. Drinking contaminated water can cause stomach illness, and some bacteria pose serious risks for children, older adults and people with weakened immune systems. Bacteria can enter through cracked well caps, poor seals, flooding or a nearby septic system that is not working properly. Nitrates and Nitrites Nitrates and nitrites often come from fertilizers, manure and septic systems. High levels are especially risky for infants, because nitrates can interfere with the blood’s ability to carry oxygen. Wells in agricultural areas or close to septic fields are more likely to be affected. Arsenic and Other Metals Arsenic occurs naturally in some rock formations and can dissolve into groundwater. It has no taste, smell or colour, and long-term exposure is linked to serious health effects. Contaminants like arsenic are important to understand precisely because they cannot be detected without testing. Other metals, such as manganese, uranium and lead from plumbing , can also be present depending on local geology and the age of the home’s pipes. Iron, Manganese and Hardness Some contaminants are mainly nuisance issues. Iron and manganese cause orange or black stains on fixtures and laundry and can give water a metallic taste. Hard water, caused by calcium and magnesium, leaves scale on taps, kettles and water heaters and reduces the effectiveness of soap. While these are not usually health hazards at typical levels, they can shorten the life of appliances and plumbing. Changes in pH can also matter. Acidic water can corrode pipes and release metals into drinking water. How Often to Test Regular testing is the only way to know what is in your water. A common recommendation is to test for bacteria at least once a year and to test for chemicals and metals every few years. Test right away after flooding, construction near the well, repairs to the well or any noticeable change in taste, smell, colour or clarity. Testing is also important when buying or selling a rural property, when someone in the household is pregnant or when treatment equipment is installed or adjusted. Use an accredited laboratory and follow its sampling instructions carefully. Many regional health authorities can recommend labs and help interpret results. How Treatment Protects Health Once you know what is in the water, the right treatment can address it. Ultraviolet disinfection systems kill bacteria and viruses without adding chemicals. Carbon filters reduce certain chemicals, odours and tastes. Specialized filters remove iron and manganese. Water softeners reduce hardness. Reverse osmosis systems, often installed at the kitchen tap, can lower levels of arsenic, nitrates and many dissolved contaminants in drinking water. The best systems are designed around test results, not guesses. Treatment equipment also needs regular maintenance, such as replacing UV lamps, filters and membranes, to keep working properly. Protecting Groundwater for the Future Private wells are directly connected to the environment around them, which makes protecting groundwater a shared responsibility. Maintaining septic systems, using fertilizers and pesticides carefully, storing fuels and chemicals safely and properly sealing unused wells all help keep aquifers clean. Choosing treatment systems that use less water and energy, and recycling or responsibly disposing of filters and equipment, can reduce the environmental footprint of clean drinking water. Healthy groundwater supports not only the households that rely on it, but also streams, wetlands and wildlife across rural regions. Health Canada provides guidance on drinking water quality, including information for private well owners. Clean Water, Peace of Mind Well water can be safe and healthy, but it requires regular attention. Testing on a schedule, understanding the results and choosing the right treatment protect your family’s health and the groundwater your home depends on. The post Common Contaminants in Private Well Water, How to Test for Them and How Treatment Protects Health appeared first on Happy Eco News .
