items.titleOriginal: Feel-Good TV Favorites: 30 Streaming Shows That’ll Brighten Your Day
items.description: Ποια είναι η συνταγή για μια καλή τηλεοπτική εκπομπή; Για κάποιους, είναι ένας συνδυασμός ρομαντισμού και χιούμορ. Για άλλους, είναι μια νοσταλγική ιστορία με συγγενείς χαρακτήρες. Και μερικές φορές συμβαίνει ακριβώς το αντίθετο: ριάλιτι απόδρασης που σε μεταφέρει κάπου μακριά. Ευτυχώς, οι ενθουσιώδεις ιστορίες όλων των ειδών είναι διαθέσιμες για ροή όλες τις ώρες της ημέρας (και της νύχτας).…
items.descriptionOriginal: What’s the recipe for a feel-good TV show? For some, it’s a mix of romance and humor. For others, it’s a nostalgic storyline with relatable characters. And sometimes it’s just the opposite: escapism reality TV that transports you somewhere far away. Luckily, uplifting stories of all kinds are available to stream at all hours of the day (and night). From comedies and coming-of-age-stories to heartwarming reality series, these shows can help you feel a little better about the world. So, make yourself a cup of tea and cozy up on the couch — a heartwarming streaming session awaits! A Man on the Inside | Netflix This is perhaps the most wholesome whodunit you’ll ever watch. In Season One, retired professor Charles (Ted Danson) goes undercover at a retirement community to investigate the theft of a family heirloom. The next season, he takes on a new case at a college campus where he meets Mona, played by Danson’s real-life wife of over 30 years, Mary Steenburgen. We’re excited to see what’s in store for Season Three, which, alas, will be this endearing tale’s final chapter . Abbott Elementary | Hulu This hilarious mockumentary series follows teachers (and an outrageous principal) at a Philadelphia public school who go above and beyond to help their students succeed, despite the hurdles the faculty encounters both in and out of the classroom. Fun fact: Abbott Elementary is named after Joyce Abbott , a real sixth-grade teacher who taught creator and star Quinta Brunson at Andrew Hamilton School in Philadelphia. All Creatures Great and Small | PBS and Prime Video All Creatures Great and Small is based on author and veterinarian James Herriot’s beloved memoirs about his years treating animals in rural Yorkshire beginning in the 1930s. The British series is so peaceful that all six seasons feel like taking a breath of fresh air (the seventh premieres in the U.S. in January 2027). Black-ish | Hulu This Emmy-winning comedy is heartwarming, family-centered, and will keep you laughing. Follow the beloved Johnsons for eight seasons as they navigate highs, lows, and life changes together. Choir | Disney+ Meet the inspiring kids who make up the Detroit Youth Choir (of America’s Got Talent fame ) in this moving Disney+ docuseries. Over six episodes, you’ll find yourself cheering on all of the talented singers as they pursue their dreams and prepare for “the performance of a lifetime”: taking the stage at Carnegie Hall in New York City. Derry Girls | Netflix Witty and wonderful, Derry Girls is a British teen sitcom that follows a tight-knit group of friends during “ The Troubles ” in Ireland. It’s a beautiful example of the power of embracing humor amid hardships, without glossing over truths. English Teacher | Hulu English Teacher is another warmhearted, witty comedy set in the classroom, and often the faculty lounge and principal’s office as well. You’ll follow a group of offbeat high school teachers in Austin, Texas, as they navigate everything from a chaotic camping trip to AI-powered trash cans. The show boasts a rating of 94% on Rotten Tomatoes, and our only complaint is that the episodes, which run just over 20 minutes, aren’t longer — because the characters are endlessly fun to be around. Extraordinary Attorney Woo | Netflix South Korean series Extraordinary Attorney Woo follows a young lawyer who is on the autism spectrum as she navigates everyday interactions in her unique and authentic way. The show, which is dubbed in English, has a 93% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes and was the most-viewed title on Netflix for a week . Gilmore Girls | Hulu For a dose of mother-daughter love, Gilmore Girls offers seven seasons (and a four-part reunion series) of feel-good content. The young mom and her teenage daughter — played by Lauren Graham and Alexis Bledel, respectively — talk fast, drink a lot of coffee, and lean on each other through family drama, job changes, and romantic ups and downs. Hart of Dixie | HBO Max If you’re a fan of Gilmore Girls , this wholesome show will be right up your alley. Rachel Bilson stars as Zoe Hart, a doctor from New York City who inherits half of a family practice in the small, fictional town of Bluebell, Alabama: a perfectly cozy community where neighbors support each other, get tangled up in romance, and attend many a quirky festival. Home for Christmas | Netflix The first season of this Norwegian show follows Johanne, a 30-year-old single nurse, as she gives herself 24 days to find a boyfriend to bring home for Christmas. Three seasons later, the show (always set during the holidays) remains full of tender moments about navigating romance, independence, and family expectations. Is It Cake? | Netflix The premise is super simple and super silly: Contestants bake elaborate cakes that look like everyday items, including purses, paintings, and rubber ducks. The desserts are then placed next to the real objects they resemble, and guest judges have to guess which one is the cake. It’s fun to play along, though it’s delightfully tricky! Love on the Spectrum U.S. | Netflix There are plenty of reality shows about finding love, but Love on the Spectrum stands out — not only because its stars are neurodivergent but also because it possesses a warmth and hopefulness that make you truly root for the cast as they seek meaningful relationships. The U.S. version is a spinoff of the Australian series , and both are available to stream on Netflix. North of North | Netflix If you need a reminder that good things can come during uncertain times, this show fits the bill. Set in the tiny, fictional Arctic community of Ice Cove, North of North follows a young Inuk mother as she embarks on a new chapter after leaving her marriage. Viewers follow along with her highs and lows as she tries to get a handle on dating and building a career, while breaking down traditional gender expectations. Psych | Prime Video and Peacock Watch a quick-witted and perceptive police consultant (played by James Roday Rodriguez) solve cases using the power of observation — and the help of his reluctant BFF (played by Dulé Hill). The eight-season show combines comedy, drama, and detective work, all the while highlighting the infectious friendship between the two main characters. Tip: Keep an eye out for pineapples ! Queer Eye | Netflix The “Fab Five” gives emotional makeovers to ordinary folks across the country. But they don’t focus on appearance alone: The team explores the powerful connection between how we look, how we treat ourselves, and how we interact with the world — a reminder we can all use. Schitt’s Creek | Hulu Riches-to-rags is the premise of Schitt’s Creek : a series about a wealthy family who loses all their money and moves into a motel in a (very) small town. Laugh-out-loud moments, endearing friendships, and perfectly quotable one-liners earned this rewatchable, lighthearted show an Emmy for outstanding comedy in 2020. Shrinking | Apple TV On paper, Shrinking doesn’t sound particularly feel-good — it follows a father (played by Jason Segel) navigating parenthood and his career as a therapist following his wife’s sudden death. However, the show portrays grief through a lens that’s undeniably uplifting. It’s impossible not to fall in love with the nosy neighbors and hilarious coworkers, especially Paul, the lovably gruff mentor played by Harrison Ford (who earned his first Emmy nomination for the role at age 83). Sister, Sister | Paramount Plus A ’90s classic, Sister, Sister — starring twins Tia and Tamera Mowry — is still a joy to watch decades after it originally aired. Equally heart-filling and funny, the six-season series captures the magic of sisterhood and the positive impact of supportive family units. Somebody Feed Phil | Netflix There are many foodie travel shows out there, but this one has Phil Rosenthal. The creator of Everybody Loves Raymond supplies just the right amount of wholesome dad jokes as he tries local cuisine in Kyoto, Copenhagen, and Cape Town, among dozens of other cities around the world. All eight seasons are packed with enticing eats and conversations, but we’re partial to the first two, which include scenes of Rosenthal video chatting with his mom and dad before they passed away in 2019 and 2021, respectively. Somebody Somewhere | Prime Video Described as “a totally platonic love story” by HBO, Somebody Somewhere is about two coworkers (played by Bridget Everett and Jeff Hiller) who become dear friends. Audiences watch as they develop the sweetest bond that’s filled with lots of laughs and good vibes. “I hope that people come away with ‘never give up on yourself,’ because a lot of people do,” said Everett. St. Denis Medical | Peacock and Netflix Think of this as a hospital-centered version of The Office (another comfort TV favorite). This sitcom chronicles the day-to-day lives of nurses and surgeons as they navigate wacky medical scenarios and even wackier workplace dynamics. But we’d be remiss not to mention that there’s plenty of heart among the staff, who lean on each other as they care for patients. Stick | Apple TV A love letter to golf, Stick follows a former pro golfer seeking redemption by mentoring a teen prodigy who has his own complicated relationship with the game. The soun d track is stacked with hits, and you’ll never listen to “Cecilia” by Simon & Garfunkel the same way again. Survivor | Netflix (Select Seasons) and Paramount Plus (All Seasons) A show that just keeps on giving, Survivor has delivered over 50 seasons of real-life drama about “castaways” competing for a prize of $1 million. While the concept has remained mostly the same for more than two decades, every season delivers new personalities and social dynamics. Ted Lasso | Apple TV The epitome of comfort TV, Ted Lasso centers on an American football coach (Jason Sudeikis) who is hired to manage a British soccer team. Even if you’re not a sports fan, this four-season series is so charming and rich with wholesome humor that makes it a feel-good favorite for everyone. Tex Mex Motors | Netflix Watch old junkyard cars from Mexico get radically restored in Texas, thanks to a talented team of experts on Tex Mex Motors . While the car transformations are fun to watch (and very impressive), the restoration pros are the real stars of the show. The Dog House | HBO Max and Hulu ​If you haven’t watched The Dog House yet, you’re in for a treat. The unscripted show follows staff at a British animal rescue charity as they match pups with new pet parents. It’s a joy watching people light up when they fall in love with their new best friend — and of course, seeing the pups fall in love with their new best friends, too. The Durrells in Corfu | PBS and Prime Video The Durrells in Corfu is a British series based on memoirs about a family who left England for Greece in the 1930s. Not only is the story full of wit and heart, but it’s also set in the dreamiest of settings. And after you watch the show’s four seasons, we recommend checking out this documentary about the real Durrells . The Great British Baking Show | Netflix Of all the comfort shows streaming lately, The Great British Baking Show (titled The Great British Bake Off in the U.K.) takes the cake — pun intended. Each week, contestants bake all kinds of mouthwatering treats in hopes of making it to the finale, where one talented baker earns the coveted cake stand and is crowned winner. But unlike so many other competition shows that can feel cutthroat, the judges offer kind, constructive feedback, and the contestants often help one another finish their creations. You can stream most seasons on Netflix, including the most recent with new judge Nigella Lawson, a star addition as far as the Nice News team is concerned. Younger | Netflix In Younger , Liza, a 40-year-old mom (played by Sutton Foster), pretends to be in her 20s to land an entry-level assistant job at a publishing house in New York alongside Kelsey (played by Hilary Duff). A love triangle, book deals, and many stories of female friendship ensue over seven seasons of lighthearted TV. Highly recommend for fans of Lizzie McGuire . A version of this article was originally published in July 2023.

items.descriptionOriginal: In the last couple of decades, many companies have reduced the heft of plastic bottles , cardboard boxes, paper envelopes, and other packaging materials, a strategy known as lightweighting. At first glance, this seems like a win-win: less material means lower costs and a lighter burden on the environment. But the approach may also backfire, a new study suggests. Researchers found that people are more likely to throw lightweight packaging away, and less likely to recycle it, compared to more substantial packaging materials. “Even well-intended sustainability practices can have unexpected negative consequences,” the researchers write. First, the researchers set out to determine the scope of the problem. A small pilot study at a university campus event and a larger week-long audit of trash and recycling bins on campus showed that lighter-weight recyclable plastic beverage containers were more likely to end up in the trash compared to more substantial plastic cups and bottles. “Once low-density packaging gets into consumers’ hands, it produces more waste, as consumers are more likely to improperly trash low-density versus high-density recyclable packaging,” the researchers write. Investigating causal relationships, the researchers concocted a laboratory study in which participants were asked to assess the properties of a piece of paper—either flimsy newsprint or sturdy cardstock—which they were instructed to dispose of at the end of the experiment. As expected, participants rated the thinner paper as lower quality than the thicker paper and were more likely to throw it in the trash at the end of the experiment—although a statistical analysis people get from recycling has a downside More details about the nuances of people’s thought processes emerged from an online experiment in which participants imagined receiving a takeout meal in either a thin paper bakery bag or a thick paper grocery bag. “Where would you put this bag?” they were asked. The participants then rated the quality of the bag, assessed its value, and indicated their level of discomfort about putting the bag in the garbage. “Ultimately, we find that consumers are more apt to throw low-density packaging in the trash because it is perceived as being more disposable (i.e., lower in value and associated with lesser feelings of waste aversion),” the researchers write. So far, so hopeless, given the human foibles and imperfect decision-making. But the solution could be a relatively simple one, according to the new work. In both an online study and a small field trial, the researchers found evidence that including a message on lightweight packaging—for example, “You may be done with this envelope, but it still has value”—increased the likelihood that the material would make it to the recycling bin. “Prompting consumers to reconsider the value of low-density packaging can curtail this unintended wastefulness,” the researchers write. Issuing such prompts is in companies’ own best interests, the researchers point out. In addition to lightweighting, many firms aim to increase the proportion of recycled material in their packaging. And where is that recycled material going to come from if consumers have thrown the previous iteration of that packaging in the trash? Source: Loomer L. and S.C. Whitley . “ Through thick and thin? When sustainable package design increases consumer waste generation .” Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science 2026. Image: © Anthropocene Magazine.

items.title: Ο πωλητής μαθαίνει την ιστορία πίσω από ένα ρυμουλκούμενο και παίρνει μια απόφαση που φέρνει μια οικογένεια σε δάκρυα
items.titleOriginal: Seller Learns the Story Behind a Tow Truck and Makes a Decision That Brings a Family to Tears
items.description: Ένας άντρας από το Μίτσιγκαν που δεν είχε την οικονομική δυνατότητα να αγοράσει πίσω το αγαπημένο ρυμουλκούμενο του παππού του, σκέφτηκε ότι είχε χάσει για πάντα την ευκαιρία του. Αλλά ο άντρας που το πουλούσε είχε άλλα σχέδια, και αυτό που έκανε στη συνέχεια έκανε μια οικογένεια σε κλάματα.
items.descriptionOriginal: A Michigan man who couldn't afford to buy back his late grandfather's beloved tow truck thought he had lost his chance forever. But the man selling it had other plans, and what he did next brought a family to tears.

items.titleOriginal: The People Who Became Wildlife
items.description: Τι μπορεί να είναι σαν να είσαι πουλί; Αρχικά η Helen Lawy πίστευε ότι το να είσαι κιρκινέζι θα σήμαινε ελευθερία. «Λατρεύω τα πουλιά, και ιδιαίτερα τα κικινέζια - όταν αιωρούνται, έχουν μια εκπληκτική εικόνα του τοπίου», λέει. Ο εξαιρετικά εύκαμπτος λαιμός και το κεφάλι του κικινέζι του δίνουν μια συναρπαστική θέα του τοπίου, ενώ τα μάτια του μπορούν να δουν εξαιρετικά…
items.descriptionOriginal: W hat might it be like to be a bird? Initially Helen Lawy thought being a kestrel would mean freedom. “I love birds, and particularly kestrels — when they’re hovering, they have an amazing overview of the landscape,” she says. The kestrel’s extraordinarily flexible neck and head give it a sweeping view of the landscape, while its eyes can see ultraviolet light, which helps it detect the urine trails left by voles. “Immediately you’ve got a very different perspective,” Lawy says animatedly. Credit: Wayne Tuckwell / Shutterstock A retired resident of Taunton, Lawy helps manage the 65-acre Longrun Meadow floodplain beside the River Tone in Somerset County, United Kingdom. When scientists asked for volunteers who wanted to attempt to view the landscape through an animal’s perspective, Lawy signed up and chose the reddish-brown kestrel, a small falcon. First she learned about the bird’s capabilities and habits. Then, over a period of several weeks, Lawy would spend hours sitting at the river’s edge and following the instructions of the “Animal Collaboration” guidebook she’d received: Sit still, pay attention, choose one sense that particularly matters to the animal. Because of the kestrels’ keen eyesight, Lawy would start with focusing on visual clues, then listen intently. “You become sort of hypervigilant,” she says. The guide — which grew out of the More Than Human Lens Toolkit , developed by anthropologist Patricia Fraga Pérez and philosopher Miguel Prado Casanova — asks people to not immediately categorize or explain what they are experiencing, but to simply notice. Once Lawy began trying to inhabit the bird’s perspective, the romantic notion of freedom disappeared. The bird needs shelter, rough grassland in which to hunt voles and mice, and space undisturbed by people and dogs. Suddenly the landscape around Lawy looked more like a series of obstacles and threats a wild animal needed to conquer: “Once I really began to delve into what it might be like to be a kestrel, I realized actually my options were very limited because it’s so difficult to find areas where I can find food.” Clatworthy dam impounds the headwaters of the River Tone. © River Tone Lawy’s experience is part of a pioneering experiment by Accelerator for Systemic Risk Assessment (ASRA), an independent nonprofit initiative hosted by the United Nations Foundation in collaboration with the University of the West of England (UWE) and funded by the Ecological Citizen(s) Network . The project, Risks Beyond Human Eyes, asks people around the River Tone catchment to explore risks not from the conventional perspective of human visitors, landowners, planners or conservationists, but through the sensory worlds and needs of other species: fierce otter, threatened salmon, quiet red deer, sharp-sighted kestrel or blind earthworm. Over a period of several months, 18 participants swam like salmon, surfed the river to mimic how an otter might glide through the water, or hid in hollows like earthworms. The setup sounds fanciful until its practical implications emerge: If conventional risk assessments systematically overlook what matters to other species, could temporarily shifting the human viewpoint reveal problems — and solutions — that would otherwise remain invisible? Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] For Lawy, it has already changed how she manages land. She came to the project as a local resident, concerned about the water quality of the River Tone. People want to bathe in it, yet the water is too polluted with runoff from the nearby fields, herbicides, pesticides and other toxins. “But animals haven’t got that choice,” she says. “They are constantly living in this very poor-quality water.” These insights are part of the logic of the ASRA project, challenging the human-centeredness of conventional risk assessment. “Of course we’re not pretending that a person literally becomes an otter or kestrel,” project co-director Phil Tovey explains, “but this kind of disciplined attention exposes aspects of an animal’s environment that humans routinely fail to notice.” The resulting testimonies are not intended simply to produce moving stories about wildlife, but are treated as input to a wider systemic-risk assessment, alongside scientific and other evidence such as water quality. Participants in the project working on a course of action. Credit: Darren Honeywell According to the 2026 Living Planet Index , freshwater species populations declined by 85 percent between 1970 and 2022 , the steepest decline of any of the major ecosystems assessed. It’s one thing to read this number as an intellectual piece of information and another to attempt the perspective of a salmon, like some of the study participants, and arrive at the life-threatening realization that they couldn’t overcome a river barrier to get to their food source. Lawy experienced firsthand that a landscape designed to look accessible and attractive to humans appears radically different to a species trying to feed and reproduce. While repeatedly sitting outside over several weeks, Lawy never actually saw a kestrel. There were too many people, too many dogs, too much disturbance. “Kestrels actually need some space from us,” she realized. Lawy also saw the hay meadows in a different light. Once the hay is cut, Lawy suddenly noticed, the landscape can become a stark, hostile expanse. “There is no cover,” she says. During a hot, dry summer, that lack of shelter can mean the difference between life and death. At the next meeting of Friends of Longrun Meadow, Lawy proposed a “mosaic of habitats,” retaining more long grass and larger riparian margins alongside the river instead of the more manicured grounds. The River Tone under the M5. © River Tone Lawy says she now asks people to adopt a new perspective. “I want you to think more from an animal perspective,” she tells them. “Rather than us thinking we need to trim that hedge, are we leaving places for birds and insects and all these other species who live here? Are we providing feeding corridors for bats?” Much to her surprise, the group “straightforwardly accepted these insights,” Lawy reports. The larger ambition of ASRA’s experiment is to translate these observations into protective action. Phil Tovey, who co-leads the project with Miguel Prado Casanova of UWE, describes the River Tone as a system in which risks compound. For instance, research has found that kestrels living within 30 meters of a major road show elevated cortisol from stress, and they shift from reproduction towards survival. “So when we then look at overall coverage of roads in the region, you can just see the scale of harm, disruption, physical and mental injury that is really widespread,” Tovey concludes. “One of the things that we do in ASRA for a systemic risk response is we look at the underlying structures, the historical conditions and what are the barriers to transformation.” A former Royal Marines Commando, Tovey served on operations across the world, from peacekeeping in Northern Ireland to working with indigenous forces in Afghanistan and deployments across Africa and the Middle East. Before joining ASRA, he worked as the Head of Futures in the U.K.’s Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs. Rain patters downstream of French Weir. © River Tone He likens the emotional testimonies of the study participants to the shocked reports of civilians caught in war zones. He also conducted roughly two dozen of his own field experiments, switching between species and testing the instructions given to participants. “I’d be going out at four in the morning, roughly knowing where the red deer hang out.” For Tovey, connecting the participants’ testimonies to scientific evidence and a structured framework for mapping risk means “setting the conditions for deeper structural change.” For example, the river and its tributaries contain more than 337 weirs and other obstacles over about 33 kilometers, creating problems for migrating salmon and other creatures. “No one has really considered the density and volume of these pressures on the animals,” Tovey says. “But when I sit as an otter, I see these barriers because as an otter I’m only about six centimeters off the ground.” Conventional assessments tend to divide problems into categories: transport, agriculture, water quality, habitat, biodiversity. Tovey’s digital mapping of the River Tone risks is effectively “bright orange” as different risks overlap. The problem is not merely the number of individual hazards, but their density and interaction. Changing the perspective does not mean abandoning scientific evidence, but it can show which actions will have the most impact. “As a research team, asking a bunch of humans to try and inevitably fail to engage in living as a chosen animal, the absurdity of trying to actually do that was taken really seriously,” says Tovey, addressing the obvious criticism of anthropomorphism. “We never once claimed that Helen was a kestrel, but using the structured process we set out, we need to make an imaginary leap to calibrate what that environment would be like for the animal. Then we start to see barriers in a different way.” The research team briefing the Systemic Risk Assessment. Credit: Darren Honeywell For Lawy, the exercise in changing perspective led to changes in land management, and then to a recognition that she wants to press for changes beyond her local group. “It’s amazing how quickly that local action on a relatively small area can lead you to realize that actually we need some policy changes within the landscape to really make that difference,” she says. The project inspired an even more ambitious question: What does the river need? One of the study participants works in the city council. According to Tovey, “she became instrumental in stitching together the work and applying it to River Tone as a subjective person.” A working group quickly formed, resulting in the adaptation of Somerset’s very first River Rights Charter, which recognizes the river’s rights to regenerate, flow and be protected from harm. Lawy’s stint as a kestrel is part of a growing global movement to shift from an anthropocentric view, inspired by programs such as NYU Law School’s More than Human Life as well as bestselling authors like Charles Foster , whose book Being A Beast portrayed him living as badger, deer, fox and swift. It also marks a return to Indigenous values. In 2008, Indigenous peoples led Ecuador to become the world’s first country to formally recognize the “Rights of Mother Earth,” a ruling that the Global Alliance for the Rights of Nature (GARN) and others subsequently used successfully against a road construction company that dumped rubble into the Vilcabamba River. As a result, the government was forced to clean up the river. Tovey agrees that rivers and other elements of nature should have the right to be represented. “I have never met my MP,” he says. “Yet we accept political representation for humans. What’s problematic is making sure it’s done with integrity.” Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime The approach remains experimental. There are obvious limits to humans attempting to understand other species, and the researchers themselves acknowledge the need for more time. But Tovey hopes to expand ASRA’s work to larger areas. “We have started to forge connections with our sister rivers, reaching out to those groups and thinking about a wider solidarity movement,” Tovey says, intending to integrate the lessons from the River Tone project. Lawy’s experience suggests another potential benefit: changing what people care about. “One of the really important things that’s come out of this for me,” she says, “is the emotional connection that you get back with nature.” That emotional connection is not taken as a substitute for evidence. Rather, it can make evidence harder to ignore. The post The People Who Became Wildlife appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Suzanne Peck , a lecturer of art at the Rochester Institute of Technology, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . Glass as a material is full of contradictions. Depending on the form and use, glass can be fragile or strong, opaque or transparent, rough or smooth. The studios my colleagues and I teach and learn in, as glass instructors, echo this abundance of physical opposites. These environments are simultaneously immersive, complex, seductive, and demanding. When the studio is in action, you might hear glass breaking, hot metal being quenched in water, glassblowing pipes rolling on the workbench rails, and some good tunes on the stereo. You might smell hot beeswax and burning newspaper. You might feel a bit of waste glass under your shoe or the intense heat from the furnaces and a breeze from a well-placed fan. Glassblowers learn to listen, to feel, and to find some focus within and among the kinetic. The constant stimuli of the glass studio may not seem anything like a sterile science lab, and yet glass artists need to accrue knowledge of physics and chemistry to achieve any kind of control with this dynamic material. They must choose a material with the desired properties and during the process judge factors such as heat and malleability. Glass as a Material At Rochester Institute of Technology, where I help run the glass program, we primarily use two types of glasses. In our hot glass studio we melt “soft” glass . This glass is specifically formulated to be melted in a furnace and used by the glassblower. It’s a combination of fine mesh silica sand, soda ash, and lime, with small amounts of a few additional ingredients that keep the glass beautiful when it’s at its top temperature of 2,200 degrees Fahrenheit (1,204 degrees Celsius). In our flameworking studio, we use a borosilicate glass . You might recognize this glass as the brand Pyrex made in Corning, New York. This is a super heat-resistant glass. It melts at a higher temperature than soft glass and arrives to our students in preformed rods that they can melt and shape by torch in our flameworking studio. The differences in chemistry really change how these glasses look and behave. Picofluidicist/Wikimedia Commons Pyrex cookware is made out of a specially formulated, heat-resistant type of glass called borosilicate. Glass, from a material science perspective, is categorized as an amorphous solid , meaning that glass’s molecules are arranged in a near-random pattern and there is no sharp melting point . Rather, glass gradually softens over a wide temperature range. Gathering Glass Once you’ve adjusted to the chaos of the studio, it’s time to start working. We have two furnaces in our hot glass studio, where we work with soft glass, so anytime during the school year there is between 700 to 1,200 pounds of glass. It’s kept in the furnace at its molten state (2,200 degrees F or 1,204 degrees C), ready to be gathered and transformed. AP Photo/Keith Srakocic Glass artists heat up their glass in a furnace so that it’s molten and easy to mold. When we work with the material, transforming it with tools and breath and heat, it needs to be kept in a workable heat zone — probably between 1,100 and 2,000 F (593 and 1,094 C). When the glass dips below that range, we perceive it as solid, though at the molecular level it is still dynamic and acting more like a liquid. To make anything — a sculpture, a tumbler, a celestial magical orb, or a pumpkin — you start by gathering glass out of the furnace on a metal rod. Once you’ve gathered your glass, you start making decisions. Elizabeth Lamark/RIT An artist works in the Glass Hot Shop at RIT. When glass is in its molten state, the artist can shape it and blow into it. You might ask yourself: What tools do I need to begin to shape and transform this glass into the object I have in mind? If you wait too long and the glass begins cooling down, you’ll need to reheat it to reintroduce malleability , allowing you to continue working it without breaking it. A big part of glasswork is moving between the reheating chamber and the bench, where the artist uses tools to move and stretch the molten glass into the desired shape. You’ll need to alternate between these two stations many times. Glassblowing is a team activity. I have physical and intellectual support from my colleagues: breath from their lungs, protection from the heat, additional bits of glass brought from the furnace to add to my object. We almost never work alone. So, say I want to make a very basic clear tumbler. This is a simple conceptual object — utilitarian, domestic, and intimate. It is also a tricky one to make well: too heavy and it feels bad in the hand, too thick at the lip and it dribbles when you drink, too thin at the bottom and it will break before it is complete. Maybe I want to design it so it is slightly conical: wider at the bottom than the top, so it’s less likely to tip over. Maybe I want it to have a little indent for the user’s thumb as a gentle invitation to her hand. First I make my design: I draw it. I share it with my team so they can predict the process and the object’s needs. Then we begin. Working With Physics I gather glass out of the furnace, let it cool a bit, then introduce a bubble in the glass by blowing into the pipe, the hollow rod that attaches to the object I’m making. I reheat, sit at the bench, and begin to shape the glass using both gravity and the Jills, a cooling and shaping tool. The Jills is kind of like a large pair of tongs. It hasn’t changed much in design for 2,000 years. AP Photo/Gerry Broome Glass artists use a variety of tools to shape their work. I ask for some air from my teammate, and she blows into the pipe while I’m shaping the glass. The bubble transforms into a pill shape, slightly wider at the bottom. I constrict the area right in front of the pipe. I’m focusing on shape and heat, taking care to not let the glass get too cold. If the glass drops to about 1,000 F (538 C), it enters a danger zone. If it’s not yet finished, it needs to be warmed up in the reheating chamber; or if it is done, put away in a kiln to cool slowly. If glass cools too quickly, the molecules freeze into a chaotic pattern, which causes stresses that result in fracture. To combat this volatility, when the glass object is done and ready to be cooled, we place the object in an annealer : a kiln set to a resting temperature of 930 F (500 C). This temperature is like a Goldilocks zone for our glass: It’s not so hot that the glass will deform, but not so cool that the glass will stress and break. Once the kilns are full, a computer guide takes them down to room temperature over about 10 hours. As I continue to work on my cup, I get more heat, focusing on the very end of the bubble — the part that will be the base of the cup. I then sit down and have another member of my team flatten the bottom with a wooden paddle while I tool the glass with the Jills to keep its shape. The cycle continues on and on. The process is quick, but also there are so many little steps that it would take nearly a full-length book to describe them all. When asked how long it takes to make a tumbler, I’ll often answer, “About 10 years or 10 minutes, depending on how you think about time and material knowledge.” This is both glib and true. Glass demands attention, dedication, and a willingness to make connections between physics and chemistry and your observable experiences. It is a highly challenging and equally rewarding material to work with and alongside. I count myself very lucky.
